cells.tense: You are keeping what passes between people even right now, and it takes no one asking twice.
cells.act: set the finished thing down in a form that keeps
cells.ask: Take an exchange that's already finished and set it down where it keeps — the terms in plain words, written once, somewhere it can be found before anyone has to recall it.
cells.core:
You can hand something over and take something in without a running tally in the back of your head, and between people that ease is holding a real arrangement steady. Both sides of the exchange stay level because you keep both sides in view, yours included. Nobody has to chase you for terms, and nobody gets handed a different deal than the one they were promised.

What still needs doing is making it keep. An exchange that's finished — a loan squared, a favor returned, a division of labor that works — set it down where it won't blur, the terms in plain words rather than in memory. Not because anyone is owed a reckoning. Because a fair arrangement remembered loosely becomes a different arrangement, quietly, and this one is worth keeping as it was.
cells.sheetLine: You give and take evenly. Give the evenness a shape that stays.
cells.verb: keeping what passes between people level
cells.place: where what's tipped between people gets set back to even

cells.tense: You are leaning toward a future where nobody's half gets dropped, and the leaning has become its own load.
cells.act: carry your own share, all of it
cells.ask: At a shared cost — money, hours, a chore nobody owns — take your half and carry it to the end, without pausing to see whether they're pulling as hard as you.
cells.core:
Fairness has started to look like something that gets guaranteed ahead of time, and that has left you watching both sides of the scale at once. Someone hesitates on their part, and you feel the whole thing tipping, so you lean in and lean in until the arrangement rests on your grip rather than on the two of you. Being carried has a weight of its own. People feel that weight, and what they feel isn't even.

Things hold better when each side holds its own. Take a shared cost — money, hours, a chore nobody owns — and carry your half all the way through without checking whether they're matching you. It may turn out nobody was dropping anything. You were the one holding both ends.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping it level by holding both sides of it.

cells.tense: You are standing at an exchange that already closed and you have not stepped through it.
cells.act: strike one thing from the list that does not serve
cells.ask: Take the list you keep about what you owe somebody and strike a line from it — the item carried past the point it earns. Leave the rest of the list alone without re-reading it.
cells.core:
There's a tally you've stopped updating and gone on reading. Something between you and someone got out of kilter, and instead of re-sorting it you stepped back from the whole exchange — the calls, the asking, the being asked. Outwardly things look settled. An account stays open at the edge of your attention, taking hours it no longer earns.

A way forward, with nobody else needed. Take something you actually want — an hour, a piece of work you keep putting off — and put it where the unfinished thing has been sitting in your head. Not a speech, not a repayment. Just the slot taken up by something that comes back to you. What ended stays ended; what's yours comes forward.

cells.tense: You are levelling things between people as they tip, while telling yourself you stay out of it.
cells.act: keep the truth a while before saying it
cells.ask: When two people near you are out of kilter, hold what you can see about each of them for a day before moving a single word or weight in either direction.
cells.core:
Somebody near you is being shorted, and the correction is already underway, and you'd say you weren't the one doing it. Your hand is on it, lightly and often — a true version reaching the right ear later, a weight shifted back toward even — and the correction keeps arriving, which means someone keeps arranging it. The fair call is being made in your house, at your table, and the one making it keeps a quieter story than the work being done.

Try this once. When two people near you are out of kilter, keep what you see about each to yourself for a day, both sides sitting with you untouched. No correction, no small true word slid in edgewise. The discomfort that shows up may not be the imbalance. It may be knowing exactly how to set it right and not being asked.

attempts.check: The draft wants to say the person is surrounded by unfair exchanges 'right now,' which the record does not support — it says the capacity has stepped back from the exchange, not what the room contains, so the Too Little core is written to locate the person behind the present without naming events. A reader could reasonably say the exchanges feel equal and fine and the cost is elsewhere; the asks survive that, since sorting one line, holding one number, and writing both sides all teach the same perception whether or not the read is right. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line that congratulates them for 'seeing clearly'; it is cut, and nothing in the cells tells them what they already know better than they do.
